headline: Plan Your Yorkshire Dales Visit and Accommodation
reservation: Entry to the park is generally open, but specific activities like the Ingleton Waterfall Trail require local access check. Accommodation varies from cosy B&Bs to holiday cottages which often require advance booking. Systems for parking or specific site access may change, so always verify with official park sources or visitor centres in Hawes, Malham, or Grassington before travel.

days.title: Limestone Scars and Cinematic Coves

stops.name: Malham Cove
stops.detail: Walk the classic limestone pavement featured in Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows.

stops.name: Gordale Scar
stops.detail: Visit this dramatic limestone gorge and waterfall, a key example of the park's unique geology.

stops.name: Janet’s Foss
stops.detail: Follow the trail to this tranquil waterfall tucked into ancient woodland near Malham.

days.driving: Allow 1 hour for local transfers; conditions vary by narrow lane widths.
days.note: Expect high foot traffic near Malham; pace for moderate walking on uneven stone.

days.title: Wensleydale Heritage and Famous Falls

stops.name: Hardraw Force
stops.detail: Observe England's longest unbroken drop waterfall, a site used in Robin Hood Prince of Thieves.

stops.name: Wensleydale Creamery
stops.detail: Explore the local cheese-making traditions in the heart of Hawes.

stops.name: Aysgarth Falls
stops.detail: View the world-famous tiered limestone waterfalls on the River Ure.

days.driving: Allow 1.5 hours; local roads are scenic but winding.
days.note: Check seasonal flow for falls; Hawes is a major supply town for this region.

days.title: High Peaks and Railway Icons
days.start: Suggested: 8 AM from Horton in Ribblesdale

stops.name: Pen-y-Ghent
stops.detail: Ascend one of the iconic Yorkshire Three Peaks for sweeping views of the moorland.

stops.name: Ribblehead Viaduct
stops.detail: Admire the 19th-century engineering of the Settle-Carlisle line cutting through the fells.

days.driving: Allow 1 hour; parking near Ribblehead can be limited.
days.note: Peak weather changes rapidly; only attempt summits with appropriate preparation.

intel.title: Village Hub Logistics
intel.text: Formal parking is available at National Park Visitor Centres in Grassington and Malham. Popular waterfall trailheads often rely on small local lots that can fill early during summer months.

intel.title: Upland Connectivity
intel.text: Mobile reception is frequently unavailable in deep valleys like Swaledale or on open moorland. Download maps before leaving gateway towns such as Skipton or Settle.

intel.title: Gateway Supplies
intel.text: Fuel stations are primarily located in larger towns like Hawes and outside the park boundaries in Skipton or Kendal. Ensure a full tank before exploring remote areas like the Buttertubs Pass.

intel.title: Peak Season Pacing
intel.text: Major sites like Aysgarth Falls attract high visitor numbers between late morning and mid-afternoon. Consider early starts to secure access at smaller limestone pavement sites.

intel.title: Terrain and Trails
intel.text: The park offers 'miles without stiles' for accessible routes, though many fell paths are rugged. Over 95% of the land is privately owned, requiring visitors to stick to designated bridleways and footpaths.

plan.arrival: First two hours: Pick up rental vehicle in Leeds or Darlington. Stop in Skipton or Settle for supplies before entering the central Dales to check into a local B&B.
plan.vehicle: Standard cars are suitable for most roads, but RVs and large campers may struggle with extremely narrow lanes and steep passes like Buttertubs; check specific rental restrictions.
plan.goldenHour: Malham Cove limestone pavement provides a dramatic sunset view, though visibility depends heavily on moorland cloud cover.
